ReLTER.inatEnrich — Technical Reference

Source: vignettes/articles/ReLTER_inatEnrich_article.Rmd
ReLTER_inatEnrich_article.Rmd

Overview

This article is a technical complement to the Getting Started vignette. It documents the internal data structures produced at each step of the enrichment pipeline, the API endpoints queried, and the recommended patterns for accessing nested list-columns in downstream analyses.

Package architecture

ReLTER.inatEnrich is structured around four public functions that operate sequentially on an sf tibble of iNaturalist occurrences:

Function Data source Output column(s)
add_iucn_to_occ() iNaturalist API /v1/taxa/{id} status_IUCN (list-column)
add_nativeness_to_occ() iNaturalist API /v1/taxa/{id} establishmentMeans (list-column)
add_legal_to_occ() BISE REST API (biodiversity.europa.eu) directive, annex (flat columns)
create_leaflet_occ_map() — Leaflet map object

All API calls use httr2 with retry logic (max_tries = 3, max_seconds = 120) and return a safe empty tibble on failure, so the pipeline never interrupts on a single taxon error.

Nested list-column structures

Two of the four enrichment functions produce list-columns — columns where each cell contains a tibble rather than a scalar value. This design allows multiple records per taxon (e.g. one IUCN assessment per geographic scope) to coexist in a single row of the occurrence tibble without information loss.

establishmentMeans

Produced by add_nativeness_to_occ(). Each cell contains a 1 × 11 tibble with the nativeness status, the authority that recorded it (filtered to the specified country), and EASIN alien species fields.

# str(occ$establishmentMeans[[1]])
tibble [1 × 11] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
 $ iNat_nativeness                    : chr "native"
 $ iNat_authority                     : chr "Italy Check List"
 $ iNat_checkList_uri                 : chr "https://www.inaturalist.org/lists/..."
 $ EASIN_url                          : chr NA
 $ EASIN_id                           : chr NA
 $ EASIN_LSID                         : chr NA
 $ EASIN_firstIntroductionsInEU_year  : chr NA
 $ EASIN_firstIntroductions_Country   : chr NA
 $ EASIN_status                       : chr NA
 $ EASIN_hasImpact                    : chr NA
 $ EASIN_IsEUConcern                  : chr NA

Accessing the values:

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

# Extract nativeness for all rows as a flat character vector
occ |>
  mutate(
    nativeness   = map_chr(establishmentMeans,
                           ~ .x$iNat_nativeness[[1]] %||% NA_character_),
    em_authority = map_chr(establishmentMeans,
                           ~ .x$iNat_authority[[1]]  %||% NA_character_)
  )

# Unnest to a flat tibble (duplicates rows where needed)
occ |>
  tidyr::unnest(establishmentMeans)

When is it NA?

iNat_nativeness and iNat_authority are both NA_character_ when:

  • the taxon has no listed taxa records in iNaturalist, or
  • none of the listed taxa records match the specified country, or
  • the API call failed after the maximum number of retries.

EASIN fields are NA when the taxon is not present in the EASIN catalogue (i.e. it is not considered an alien species in Europe).

status_IUCN

Produced by add_iucn_to_occ(). Each cell contains an N × 4 tibble, with one row per geographic scope for which an IUCN assessment exists. The number of rows varies by taxon.

# str(occ$status_IUCN[[1]])
tibble [3 × 4] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
 $ status            : chr [1:3] "LC" "LC" "LC"
 $ authority         : chr [1:3] "IUCN Red List" "IUCN Red List" "IUCN Red List"
 $ scope_of_assesment: chr [1:3] "Globally" "Europe" "Mediterranean"
 $ url               : chr [1:3] "https://www.iucnredlist.org/..."
                                 "https://www.iucnredlist.org/..."
                                 "https://www.iucnredlist.org/..."

The scope_of_assesment field identifies the geographic scope of the assessment:

  • "Globally" — global assessment
  • "Europe", "Mediterranean", etc. — regional assessments

Accessing the values:

# Extract only the global status (scope_of_assesment is "Globally")
occ |>
  mutate(
    iucn_global = map_chr(status_IUCN, function(tbl) {
      global <- tbl |> filter(scope_of_assesment == "Globally")
      if (nrow(global) == 0) NA_character_ else global$status[[1]]
    })
  )

# Extract all scopes as a flat tibble (one row per taxon × scope)
occ |>
  select(taxon.id, name, status_IUCN) |>
  tidyr::unnest(status_IUCN)

# Get all distinct statuses for a single taxon
occ$status_IUCN[[1]] |>
  select(scope_of_assesment, status, url)

IUCN status codes reference:

Code Meaning
EX Extinct
EW Extinct in the Wild
CR Critically Endangered
EN Endangered
VU Vulnerable
NT Near Threatened
LC Least Concern
DD Data Deficient
NE Not Evaluated

directive and annex (flat columns)

Produced by add_legal_to_occ(). Unlike the IUCN and nativeness data, EU legal information is stored as flat character columns. When a taxon is covered by more than one directive or annex, the occurrence tibble contains multiple rows for the same observation — one per directive/annex combination.

# Example: a taxon covered by both directives
# A tibble: 2 × (n + 2)
#   taxon.id  ...  directive                              annex
#   <int>          <chr>                                  <chr>
# 1 48484          Birds Directive (2009/147/EC)          I
# 2 48484          Habitats Directive (92/43/EEC)         IV

Annex values by directive:

For the Habitats Directive, annex values follow the standard format: "II", "II*" (priority species), "IV", "V", or combinations.

For the Birds Directive, annex values reflect the structure of the directive itself: "I" (special protection areas).

These values are parsed from the BISE Protection table, which returns full English descriptions (e.g. "Annex IV: animal and plant species of community interest in need of strict protection."). The parser extracts the Roman numeral code ("IV") using a regular expression.

Note: The BISE API returns EU-wide data only — annex assignments are not filtered by country. All annexes applicable to the species across the EU are returned. This means that row count in occ_eLTER_legal may exceed row count in occ_eLTER_nativeness for taxa with multiple directive entries. Keep this in mind when computing summaries.

# Count unique observations (not rows) correctly
n_obs <- occ_eLTER_legal |>
  dplyr::distinct(taxon.id, observed_on, user.login) |>
  nrow()

# Summarise directives per taxon without duplicating observations
directives_per_taxon <- occ_eLTER_legal |>
  dplyr::select(taxon.id, directive, annex) |>
  dplyr::distinct() |>
  dplyr::group_by(taxon.id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_directives = sum(!is.na(directive)),
    directives   = paste(na.omit(directive), collapse = "; "),
    annexes      = paste(na.omit(annex),     collapse = "; "),
    .groups      = "drop"
  )

API details

iNaturalist API

Both add_iucn_to_occ() and add_nativeness_to_occ() query the iNaturalist v1 taxa endpoint:

GET https://api.inaturalist.org/v1/taxa/{taxon_id}

The relevant fields extracted from the response are:

  • results[[1]]$conservation_statuses → IUCN status, authority, URL
  • results[[1]]$listed_taxa → establishment means, place name, list title

Both functions iterate over unique taxon IDs only, so each taxon is queried exactly once regardless of how many observations exist for it in the dataset.

Rate limiting: the iNaturalist API applies rate limiting to unauthenticated requests (approximately 60 requests per minute). The functions include a short delay between requests (Sys.sleep(0.1), approximately 6 req/sec) to stay well within this limit. The built-in retry logic (max_tries = 3, max_seconds = 120) handles any transient failures gracefully.

BISE REST API

get_eunis_legal_info() (called by add_legal_to_occ()) queries the BISE (Biodiversity Information System for Europe) REST API at https://biodiversity.europa.eu using two sequential POST requests:

Step 1 — Species name → id_eunis:

POST https://biodiversity.europa.eu/++api++/data/all-species-search-listing/@connector-data
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "data_query": [
    {
      "i": "scientific_name",
      "o": "plone.app.querystring.operation.string.contains",
      "v": "Canis lupus"
    }
  ],
  "form": {"db_version": "latest"}
}

The response contains parallel arrays under data.results (e.g. id_eunis, scientific_name). The exact-match row is selected by comparing scientific_name case-insensitively; the first result is used as a fallback.

Step 2 — id_eunis → legal status (Protection table):

POST https://biodiversity.europa.eu/++api++/data/natura-2000-species-legal-status/@connector-data
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "data_query": [
    {
      "i": "id_eunis",
      "o": "plone.app.querystring.operation.selection.any",
      "v": ["1367"]
    }
  ],
  "form": {"db_version": "latest"}
}

The response parallel arrays include legal_instrument, annex, url_link, and id_eunis. Only rows where legal_instrument is "EU Habitats Directive" or "EU Birds Directive" are retained.

The annex field contains full descriptions such as:

"Annex IV: animal and plant species of community interest in need of strict protection."

These are parsed to short codes ("IV") using the regular expression sub("^Annex\\s+(I{1,3}V?|VI?|IV|V?I{0,3}).*", "\\1", annex_str).

Throttling: add_legal_to_occ() inserts a 200 ms pause between taxa (Sys.sleep(0.2)) to avoid overloading the BISE server.

Error handling and NA semantics

All three enrichment functions use the same defensive pattern:

# Conceptual structure shared by all enrichment functions
result <- tryCatch(
  query_external_api(taxon.id),
  error = function(e) {
    warning("Error for taxon.id: ", taxon.id, " — ", conditionMessage(e))
    return(empty_fallback_tibble)   # never returns NULL
  }
)

This guarantees that:

  1. The pipeline always completes even if individual API calls fail
  2. Failed taxa are identifiable by NA values in the enrichment columns
  3. A warning() is emitted for each failure, visible in the R console

annex = NA semantics: a taxon may have a valid directive entry but annex = NA. This means the taxon is present in the BISE Protection table as covered by that directive, but no annex code could be parsed from the BISE description string. This is rare but can occur for entries with non-standard formatting.

To inspect which taxa failed or have missing data after running the pipeline:

# Taxa with no IUCN data
occ |>
  filter(map_lgl(status_IUCN, ~ all(is.na(.x$status))))

# Taxa with no nativeness data
occ |>
  filter(map_lgl(establishmentMeans, ~ is.na(.x$iNat_nativeness[[1]])))

# Taxa with no EU legal data
occ |>
  filter(is.na(directive)) |>
  distinct(taxon.id, name)

# Taxa with directive but no annex resolved
occ |>
  filter(!is.na(directive), is.na(annex)) |>
  distinct(taxon.id, name, directive)

Performance considerations

For large occurrence datasets (> 1 000 unique taxa), the enrichment functions can take several minutes due to the sequential nature of the API calls and the retry logic. A few practical tips:

  • Cache intermediate results between steps using saveRDS() / readRDS() to avoid re-querying on re-runs:
# Save after the slowest step
saveRDS(occ_eLTER_IUCN,      "cache/occ_eLTER_IUCN.rds")
saveRDS(occ_eLTER_nativeness, "cache/occ_eLTER_nativeness.rds")
saveRDS(occ_eLTER_legal,      "cache/occ_eLTER_legal.rds")

# Reload
occ_eLTER_legal <- readRDS("cache/occ_eLTER_legal.rds")
  • Rate limits: the iNaturalist API does not require authentication for read-only taxon queries, but it does apply rate limiting. The built-in per-request delay and retry logic handle this automatically; no manual throttling is needed in user code. For BISE, the 200 ms inter-taxon delay in add_legal_to_occ() is sufficient for typical dataset sizes.
